query: What are the best practices and industry standards for LLM-based "deep research" systems — agentic systems that decompose a question, run iterative tool-augmented search, and produce cited synthesis reports?
instructions:
AUDIENCE
Technically-literate practitioner who is building, evaluating, or hardening an LLM deep-research system (e.g. an agent that plans sub-questions, fans out parallel web searches/fetches, and synthesizes a cited report). Assume familiarity with LLMs, RAG, tool use, and basic agent loops. Do not explain what an LLM is. Do explain non-obvious tradeoffs.

SCOPE
In scope:
  - Architecture patterns for deep-research agents: planner/worker decomposition, lead-agent + subagent fan-out (Anthropic's pattern), single-agent ReAct loops, tree-of-thought / iterative deepening, memory/scratchpad design.
  - Production systems to compare and learn from: OpenAI Deep Research, Anthropic Claude Research / multi-agent research system, Google Gemini Deep Research, Perplexity Deep Research, You.com, plus notable open-source (GPT-Researcher, OpenDeepResearch, smolagents-based, LangGraph deep-research templates, Hugging Face open Deep Research).
  - Sub-question planning and decomposition: breadth vs depth, when to recurse, stopping criteria, budget/iteration caps.
  - Retrieval & browsing: search API choice, query reformulation, dedup, freshness, robots/ToS, handling paywalls and PDFs, JS-rendered pages.
  - Grounding and citations: inline numbered citations, span-level attribution, hallucinated-citation detection, "confidence" labels, source diversity requirements.
  - Evaluation: which benchmarks matter (BrowseComp, GAIA, HELM, Humanity's Last Exam, FRAMES, FreshQA, SimpleQA), LLM-as-judge graders, citation faithfulness metrics (e.g. Attributable to Identified Sources / AIS), human eval protocols, regression test design for agents.
  - Safety and abuse: indirect prompt injection / XPIA from fetched pages, exfiltration risks (lethal trifecta: private data + untrusted content + outbound comms), data-leak guards, refusal patterns, sandboxing browsing.
  - Cost, latency, and reliability: token budgets, parallelism, caching, model cascades (cheap planner + strong synthesizer), retry/timeout policy, partial-result handling.
  - Prompting and context engineering specific to research agents: system prompt structure, tool descriptions, "lost in the middle" mitigations, context compaction, structured intermediate artifacts.

Out of scope:
  - General consumer "prompt engineering" tips for ChatGPT.
  - Pure RAG-over-private-corpus systems with no web search and no agentic planning.
  - Full surveys of LLM training or alignment unrelated to research agents.

SOURCE PREFERENCES
Strongly prefer (cite these where they exist):
  - Engineering blog posts and system cards from the labs that ship these products: Anthropic (especially the multi-agent research system engineering post and Claude system cards), OpenAI (Deep Research launch + system card), Google DeepMind / Google blog (Gemini Deep Research), Perplexity engineering posts.
  - arXiv / peer-reviewed papers on agentic search, multi-agent LLMs, BrowseComp, GAIA, FRAMES, AIS / attribution evaluation, Self-RAG, Search-Augmented LLMs, ReAct, Reflexion, Tree-of-Thoughts.
  - Reputable engineering write-ups: LangChain/LangGraph blog, Hugging Face blog (open Deep Research), Simon Willison's notes on prompt injection and the "lethal trifecta", official LLM-eval framework docs (HELM, Inspect, OpenAI Evals).

Acceptable but secondary: well-sourced technical journalism (The Information, Sequoia, a16z) for product comparisons; vendor docs.

Avoid: SEO listicle blogs ("Top 10 AI research tools 2024"), Medium posts with no primary citations, marketing pages without technical detail, undated content.

For every non-trivial claim, prefer a primary source (lab blog, paper, official docs) over a secondary recap.

GEOGRAPHY / TIME
Global. Heavily weight 2024–2026 material — the deep-research product category effectively started in late 2024 (Gemini Deep Research Dec 2024, OpenAI Deep Research Feb 2025, Perplexity Deep Research Feb 2025, Anthropic multi-agent research system writeup mid-2025). Older foundational papers (ReAct 2022, Self-RAG 2023, AIS 2021) are fine when they're the canonical reference.

OUTPUT FORMAT
Structured Markdown report with these top-level sections, in this order:
  1. Executive summary (≤8 bullets, each one practice + why).
  2. Reference architectures — diagrams-in-prose comparing single-agent vs orchestrator-worker vs hierarchical planner; concrete examples from named systems.
  3. Planning & decomposition — breadth/depth, recursion, budget caps, stopping rules, with empirical numbers where available (e.g. Anthropic's reported token-use multipliers, parallel subagent counts).
  4. Retrieval & browsing — search backends, query rewriting, source dedup/diversity, freshness, PDFs.
  5. Grounding & citations — citation styles, faithfulness/attribution metrics (AIS, citation-F1), hallucinated-citation detection, confidence labeling.
  6. Evaluation — benchmarks (BrowseComp, GAIA, FRAMES, HLE, SimpleQA, FreshQA), LLM-judge protocols, regression strategy for non-deterministic agents.
  7. Safety & abuse — indirect prompt injection, lethal-trifecta exfiltration, sandboxing, allowlists, output filtering.
  8. Cost, latency, reliability — model cascades, parallelism, caching, partial-result handling, observability.
  9. Open problems & disagreements — places where labs/practitioners visibly disagree (e.g. multi-agent vs strong-single-agent, when long context replaces RAG, citation UX).
  10. Concrete checklist — a numbered "if you're building one tomorrow" checklist of ~15 items.

Use inline numbered citations like [1], [2] tied to a numbered References section at the end. For each cited claim, include a confidence label (High / Medium / Low) reflecting source quality and corroboration. Note publication dates next to each reference.

COMPLETENESS CHECKLIST (the report MUST address each)
  [ ] Names and briefly characterizes architectures of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Perplexity deep-research systems with primary-source citations.
  [ ] Reports concrete numbers from Anthropic's multi-agent research engineering post (token usage vs single-agent, performance lift, parallel subagent counts) if available.
  [ ] Discusses orchestrator-worker vs single-agent tradeoffs explicitly.
  [ ] Lists at least 4 evaluation benchmarks relevant to deep research and what each measures.
  [ ] Covers citation faithfulness metrics (AIS or equivalent) and hallucinated-citation detection.
  [ ] Addresses indirect prompt injection from fetched web pages and the "lethal trifecta" exfiltration pattern.
  [ ] Covers cost/latency mitigations (parallelism, model cascade, caching) with at least one quantitative anchor.
  [ ] Notes at least 2 substantive disagreements or open questions in the field.
  [ ] Ends with a 15-ish-item concrete build checklist.
  [ ] Flags any claim where sources conflict or evidence is thin.

LENGTH
Aim for a thorough report (target ~3,000–5,000 words of body text). Depth over breadth — better to cite one primary source well than three listicles.

What concrete techniques do primary sources (arXiv papers on ReAct, Self-RAG, Reflexion, Tree-of-Thoughts; LangGraph/LangChain, Hugging Face Open Deep Research, GPT-Researcher, smolagents engineering write-ups) recommend for sub-question planning and decomposition in deep-research agents — specifically breadth-vs-depth tradeoffs, recursion criteria, iteration/budget caps, stopping rules, and scratchpad/memory design?

What are the current best practices for retrieval, browsing, and citation grounding in deep-research agents — including search backend selection, query rewriting, source deduplication and diversity, freshness handling, PDF/JS-rendered page extraction, inline citation styles, and citation-faithfulness metrics such as Attributable to Identified Sources (AIS), citation-F1, and hallucinated-citation detection — based on primary papers and lab engineering posts?

Which evaluation benchmarks and protocols are considered authoritative for deep-research agents — specifically BrowseComp, GAIA, FRAMES, Humanity's Last Exam, SimpleQA, FreshQA, and HELM — what does each measure, what scores have leading systems reported, and what LLM-as-judge and human-eval protocols (including regression testing for non-deterministic agents) are documented in their original papers and official leaderboards?

findings.sub_question: What are the documented architectures, orchestration patterns, and quantitative engineering details (token-use multipliers, parallel subagent counts, performance lifts, model cascades) of the production deep research systems from Anthropic (Claude multi-agent research system), OpenAI (Deep Research), Google (Gemini Deep Research), and Perplexity Deep Research, according to their own engineering blog posts, system cards, and official documentation in 2024–2026?
findings.summary:
All four production deep-research systems share a common high-level shape — a planning/decomposition stage, an iterative tool-augmented search/reason loop, and a final cited-synthesis stage — but they differ sharply in orchestration topology and the engineering trade-offs they expose. Anthropic's Claude Research (Jun 2025 engineering blog) is explicitly an orchestrator-worker multi-agent system: a Claude Opus 4 LeadResearcher decomposes the query, persists a plan to an external Memory (to survive 200K-token context truncation), spawns 3–5 Claude Sonnet 4 subagents in parallel — each running its own OODA loop with 3+ parallel tool calls and its own context window — and then a separate CitationAgent attributes claims to sources. Quantitatively, the Opus-4-lead/Sonnet-4-subagent configuration outperforms single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research eval; token usage alone explains ~80% of variance on BrowseComp (token-count, tool-call count, and model choice together explain ~95%). Multi-agent runs burn ~15× the tokens of chat (vs. ~4× for single-agent), parallelization cut research time up to 90%, and a self-improving tool-description agent yielded a 40% drop in task-completion time. Effort scaling is hard-coded in prompts: 1 agent / 3–10 calls for fact-finding, 2–4 subagents / 10–15 calls for comparisons, 10+ subagents for complex research. Subagents are run synchronously today; deployments use 'rainbow' traffic shifts to avoid breaking long-running agents.

OpenAI Deep Research (Feb 2025 launch + system card) takes the opposite topological choice: a single agentic model — an early version of o3 optimized for web browsing — is trained end-to-end via reinforcement learning on browsing tasks (search/click/scroll/file-interpretation plus a sandboxed Python tool with no internet access). There is no parallel subagent fan-out described; instead, capability scales with test-time compute and 'max tool calls' per run (5–30 minutes wall-clock per query). A second, custom-prompted o3-mini model summarizes the chain of thought for the user. Quantitative lifts: Humanity's Last Exam 26.6% (vs. o1 9.1%, o3-mini-high 13.0%), GAIA 67.36 pass@1 / 72.57 cons@64 (state of the art at release), SWE-bench Verified 68% (+20 pts over o1), and a measurable monotonic relationship between max tool calls and pass-rate on internal expert tasks. The Preparedness Framework rated Deep Research 'Medium' risk across all four tracked categories (cybersecurity, CBRN, persuasion, model autonomy) — the first model rated medium on cybersecurity. Mitigations include refusing arbitrary URL construction (to block API-key exfiltration via prompt injection), with prompt-injection attack-success rate driven from 3–18% pre-mitigation to ~0–2.6% post-mitigation. Rate limits started at 100 queries/month for Pro; an o4-mini-based 'lightweight' variant later expanded access (250/month Pro, 25/month Plus, 5/month Free). The Feb 2026 update added MCP/app connectors and trusted-site restriction.

Google Gemini Deep Research (Dec 2024 launch, plus Dec 2025 Interactions API and Apr 2026 Deep Research/Deep Research Max) is architecturally closest to the Anthropic pattern in spirit but uses a single planner that orchestrates concurrent task models rather than spawning independent agents. Components: (1) a multi-step planner that produces a user-editable research plan; (2) task models that the planner schedules — explicitly 'intelligently determines which sub-tasks can be tackled simultaneously and which need to be done sequentially'; (3) a synthesis stage with self-critique passes. A 'novel asynchronous task manager' maintains shared state between planner and task models so single failures don't restart the run, and the system uses Gemini's 1M-token context plus a RAG layer to retain hundreds of pages browsed within a session. Model cascade is unusually explicit: launched on Gemini 1.5 Pro → upgraded to Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking (cited as both quality and serving-efficiency improvement enabling much wider access) → Gemini 3 Pro for the Dec 2025 Interactions-API agent (HLE 46.4%, DeepSearchQA 66.1%, BrowseComp 59.2%) → Gemini 3.1 Pro for Apr 2026's two-SKU split: 'Deep Research' (low-latency, interactive) and 'Deep Research Max' (extended test-time compute for asynchronous, comprehensive runs). Google's own DeepSearchQA paper notes pass@8 substantially exceeds pass@1, validating parallel trajectory exploration. The agent integrates Google Search, MCP servers, URL Context, Code Execution, File Search, and (in 2026) native chart/infographic generation.

Perplexity Deep Research (launched Feb 14, 2025) is the most opaque architecturally but explicitly positions itself as a single-agent iterative loop on top of Perplexity's AI-first search stack, branded later as the 'Sonar Deep Research' model. Per the launch blog: it 'performs dozens of searches, reads hundreds of sources, and reasons through the material,' iteratively searching, reading, and refining a plan, then synthesizing a report — typically completing in 2–4 minutes (vs. 5–30 minutes for OpenAI/Google). Reported benchmarks: Humanity's Last Exam 21.1% (above Gemini Thinking, o3-mini, o1, DeepSearchR1 at the time of launch but well below OpenAI Deep Research's 26.6%) and SimpleQA 93.9%. The retrieval substrate is described in Perplexity's own April 2026 'How Perplexity Builds Accuracy' post and Sept 2025 search-API article: hybrid keyword+semantic retrieval, multi-stage ranking (a fast recall step in 100–200 ms followed by slower rerankers), and a 'content understanding' module that segments pages into spans used as first-class retrieval units. Their post-training pipeline trains the answer model in two stages — instruction/tool behavior first, harder search/synthesis tasks second — and uses rubric-based rewards for open-ended tasks plus a discipline term that penalizes search steps and tokens that don't measurably improve the answer. Pricing/availability documented in third-party sources (5 free queries/day, 500/day for Pro at launch); a Feb 2026 internal benchmark, DRACO, was released to measure deep-research accuracy/completeness/objectivity.

Cross-cutting patterns from primary sources: (i) every system implements a plan → iterate (search/read/reason) → synthesize → cite pipeline; (ii) Anthropic and Google explicitly support parallelism (Anthropic via subagents, Google via planner-scheduled concurrent tasks), while OpenAI and Perplexity at launch describe primarily sequential single-agent loops scaled by test-time compute; (iii) all four use a smaller/cheaper companion model somewhere — OpenAI's o3-mini for chain-of-thought summarization, Google's Flash variants for efficiency, Anthropic's Sonnet for subagents under an Opus lead, and Perplexity's lighter chat models for non-deep tasks; (iv) memory/state durability is a recurring engineering theme (Anthropic's external Memory store, Google's asynchronous task manager with shared state, OpenAI's safety system blocking URL-construction-based exfiltration); (v) reported cost is dominated by token usage that scales with 'depth' — Anthropic quantifies ~15× chat baseline for multi-agent, OpenAI calls Deep Research 'very compute intensive' and rate-limits accordingly, Google explicitly markets Deep Research Max as paying for more extended test-time compute, and Perplexity charges per-query plus per-token in its API.

OpenAI's internal expert-task evaluation showed pass-rate increases monotonically with 'max tool calls,' confirming that giving the agent more browsing/thinking budget improves quality.

Google Gemini Deep Research uses a planner that produces a user-editable research plan, then orchestrates task models that run sub-tasks in parallel where possible and sequentially when dependencies require it, followed by a synthesis stage with self-critique passes.
Google built an 'asynchronous task manager' that maintains shared state between the planner and task models, allowing graceful error recovery without restarting the entire research task.
Gemini Deep Research uses Gemini's 1M-token context window combined with a RAG setup so the agent retains content browsed across a session.

Gemini Deep Research's model cascade evolved from Gemini 1.5 Pro (Dec 2024 launch) to Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking (cited as improving both quality and serving efficiency, enabling broader access), to Gemini 3 Pro (Dec 2025 Interactions-API release) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (Apr 2026, splitting into 'Deep Research' and 'Deep Research Max' SKUs).
On the Dec 2025 Interactions-API release, Gemini Deep Research reported state-of-the-art Humanity's Last Exam 46.4%, DeepSearchQA 66.1%, and BrowseComp 59.2%.

Google's DeepSearchQA benchmark contains 900 hand-crafted 'causal chain' tasks across 17 fields, and Google reports that pass@8 substantially exceeds pass@1, demonstrating the value of running multiple parallel trajectories for verification.

Apr 2026's 'Deep Research Max' is described by Google as leveraging 'extended test-time compute to iteratively reason, search and refine' for asynchronous workflows, while the standard 'Deep Research' SKU is optimized for interactive low-latency use; both are built on Gemini 3.1 Pro and add MCP support, native chart/infographic generation, and collaborative plan editing.

Perplexity Deep Research (Feb 14, 2025 launch) iteratively searches, reads documents, and reasons through results, refining its plan, then synthesizes a report — typically completing in 2–4 minutes per query.
Perplexity Deep Research scored 21.1% on Humanity's Last Exam and 93.9% on SimpleQA at launch, beating Gemini Thinking, o3-mini, o1, and DeepSeek-R1 on HLE but trailing OpenAI Deep Research's 26.6%.
Perplexity made Deep Research free with daily caps (5 queries/day for non-subscribers, 500/day for Pro) — substantially higher per-user volume than OpenAI's monthly caps.

Perplexity's underlying retrieval stack uses hybrid (keyword + semantic) retrieval with multi-stage ranking (a fast recall step under ~100–200 ms followed by slower rerankers) and a 'content understanding' module that segments pages into spans used as first-class retrieval units.

Perplexity post-trains its answer model in two stages — first instruction/tool behavior, then harder search and synthesis tasks — and uses rubric-based rewards for open-ended tasks plus a discipline term that penalizes search steps and tokens that do not measurably improve the answer.

Anthropic's evaluation philosophy combines small-N (~20 queries) early-stage iteration, an LLM-as-judge with a single 0.0–1.0 score plus pass/fail (rubric: factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency), and human evaluation to catch source-quality biases (e.g., SEO content farms over academic PDFs).
Anthropic deploys agent updates using 'rainbow deployments' — gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while running both — to avoid breaking long-running stateful agents in flight.

Anthropic notes its lead agents currently invoke subagents synchronously, creating bottlenecks (the lead can't steer subagents mid-flight, and the run blocks on the slowest subagent); asynchronous execution is identified as a future direction.

findings.sub_question: What concrete techniques do primary sources (arXiv papers on ReAct, Self-RAG, Reflexion, Tree-of-Thoughts; LangGraph/LangChain, Hugging Face Open Deep Research, GPT-Researcher, smolagents engineering write-ups) recommend for sub-question planning and decomposition in deep-research agents — specifically breadth-vs-depth tradeoffs, recursion criteria, iteration/budget caps, stopping rules, and scratchpad/memory design?
findings.summary:
Across the cited primary sources a clear architectural pattern has converged for sub-question planning in deep-research agents: a three-phase pipeline of (1) scoping/clarification, (2) iterative recursive research, and (3) final synthesis, with explicit numeric knobs for breadth, depth, and per-stage iteration caps, plus reflection-driven stopping rules. ReAct (Yao et al., arXiv 2210.03629) established the foundational scratchpad pattern — interleaved Thought/Action/Observation traces where 'thoughts' explicitly decompose goals ('I need to search x, find y, then find z'), track sub-goal progress, and reformulate queries on failure; ReAct also pioneered hard step caps (7 steps for HotpotQA, 5 for FEVER, chosen empirically because additional steps did not improve accuracy) and a fallback-on-failure stopping rule (back off to CoT self-consistency when steps are exhausted, and back off to ReAct when CoT-SC majority is below n/2). Reflexion (Shinn et al., arXiv 2303.11366) layered an episodic 'verbal RL' memory on top: an actor (often a ReAct agent) plus an evaluator plus a self-reflection generator that writes natural-language critiques into an episodic buffer; trials are repeated up to a configurable num_trials cap, and the reference implementation exposes four memory strategies (NONE / LAST_ATTEMPT / REFLEXION / LAST_ATTEMPT_AND_REFLEXION) that explicitly separate short-term trajectory from long-term reflective memory. Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al., arXiv 2305.10601) generalized this to deliberate search over 'coherent units of text', using BFS or DFS controllers, an LLM-as-evaluator (value or vote scoring) to prune branches, and explicit branching/depth hyperparameters with the ability to look-ahead and backtrack. Self-RAG (Asai et al., arXiv 2310.11511) provides a complementary fine-grained recursion criterion: instead of a fixed per-step retrieval, the model emits Retrieve={yes,no,continue} reflection tokens segment-by-segment, and the inference algorithm exposes a soft retrieval threshold δ over the normalized P(Retrieve=Yes) plus tree-decoding with critique-token-weighted segment-level beam search (beam size B over K retrieved passages) that scores partial outputs by ISREL/ISSUP/ISUSE — so 'budget' becomes a per-segment, learned decision rather than a global counter.

The production deep-research systems all instantiate these patterns with concrete numeric knobs. GPT-Researcher's deep-research skill (assafelovic/gpt-researcher) is the most explicit: DEEP_RESEARCH_BREADTH (default 3–4) controls parallel paths per level, DEEP_RESEARCH_DEPTH (default 2) controls recursion levels, DEEP_RESEARCH_CONCURRENCY (default 4) is an asyncio semaphore, and the recursion explicitly halves breadth at each level (`new_breadth = max(2, breadth // 2)`) and decrements depth, terminating when depth ≤ 1. Each branch summarizes raw search results into 'learnings' with URL citations and 'follow-up questions' that become the next level's query (`next_query = previous research goal + follow-up questions`). A hard 25,000-word context cap (MAX_CONTEXT_WORDS) is enforced via trim_context_to_word_limit, which keeps the most recent items — an explicit budget on scratchpad size, separate from step caps. Other defaults: MAX_ITERATIONS=3 for query expansion, MAX_SUBTOPICS=3, MAX_SEARCH_RESULTS_PER_QUERY=5. Hugging Face's Open Deep Research (smolagents) uses a manager CodeAgent (max_steps=12, planning_interval=4) that delegates to a ToolCallingAgent search_agent (max_steps=20, planning_interval=4); the engineering rationale is that code-actions are ~30% fewer steps than JSON tool-calls (citing Wang et al. 2024), and code variables provide native scratchpad/state for multimodal artifacts.

LangGraph/LangChain Open Deep Research (per a detailed step-by-step walkthrough) and the analogous DeerFlow, dzhng/deep-research, and OpenDeepResearcher implementations converge on a 'supervisor + isolated sub-agents' multi-agent pattern. The supervisor is bound to three tool schemas — think_tool (reflection), conduct_research (spawn sub-agent subgraph), and ResearchComplete (terminate) — using a 'manual tool-use' pattern where conduct_research spawns parallel research subgraphs whose results are returned as compact summaries rather than added to the supervisor's message history (explicitly to avoid context-window bloat). Each sub-agent has its own subgraph (researcher → research_tools → compress_research), its own message buffer, and its own iteration counter. Stopping rules are layered: supervisor calls think_tool before every decision and emits ResearchComplete when reflection deems coverage sufficient; a hard research_iterations counter prevents runaway recursion; sub-agents call their own research_complete when their topic is exhausted; compress_research compresses raw search dumps before returning. DeerFlow adds an explicit human-in-the-loop plan-modification step and a max plan-count cap. dzhng/deep-research exposes user-facing depth/breadth/isReport parameters and recursively halves breadth and decrements depth at each level, mirroring GPT-Researcher. OpenDeepResearcher (Shumer) uses a simpler iterative loop: 4 parallel queries per round, asynchronous search + LLM relevance filter + extractor + global memory aggregation; the LLM itself decides whether to issue new queries or emit 'done' as the stopping rule, with a hard max-iteration cap as backstop.

Common recommendations that emerge from triangulation across these sources: (a) make breadth and depth explicit configurable hyperparameters and decay them over recursion (typically halve breadth, decrement depth); (b) separate 'scratchpad' (raw thought+action+observation trace within a step/sub-agent) from 'long-term memory' (compressed learnings, reflections, citations) and pass only the compressed form upward; (c) enforce *both* a hard step/iteration cap (ReAct's 7 for HotpotQA; smolagents max_steps=12/20; supervisor research_iterations) *and* a soft reflection-based stopping rule (think_tool / Reflexion self-evaluation / Self-RAG ISUSE token / 'done' from LLM); (d) use a planning_interval (smolagents' value 4) to re-plan periodically rather than only at the start; (e) summarize/compress retrieved content before storing it in working memory (Self-RAG segment summarization, dzhng's 'learnings', LangGraph compress_research, GPT-Researcher's process_research_results); (f) deliver findings (information) rather than finished prose between sub-agents and the report writer to preserve coherence in the final synthesis; and (g) provide a soft retrieval/budget knob (Self-RAG's δ threshold; reasoning_effort = low/medium/high in GPT-Researcher and Open Deep Research) so users can trade quality against cost.

key_facts.claim: ReAct prompts include explicit decomposition thoughts of the form 'I need to search x, find y, then find z' and use thoughts to track progress, reformulate queries, and synthesize answers — making the thought stream the agent's working-memory scratchpad.

ReAct uses an empirically chosen hard step cap (7 steps for HotpotQA, 5 for FEVER) because more steps were shown not to improve performance, and falls back to CoT self-consistency when ReAct fails to return an answer within the cap; conversely it falls back to ReAct from CoT-SC when the majority answer occurs in fewer than n/2 of n samples.

ReAct's most common failure mode is reasoning-loop / repetitive thoughts (≈47% of failures on HotpotQA), with non-informative search accounting for ≈23%; the authors suggest beam-search decoding as a mitigation — motivating tree-search successors.

Self-RAG makes retrieval an adaptive, per-segment decision: the model emits a Retrieve∈{yes, no, continue} token at each segment, and a configurable threshold δ on the normalized probability of Retrieve=Yes lets users tune retrieval frequency without retraining.

Self-RAG uses segment-level beam search (beam size B over K retrieved passages) where the score is a weighted linear sum of normalized critique-token probabilities (ISREL, ISSUP, ISUSE), giving a soft, multi-criterion stopping/selection rule rather than a global iteration cap.

Reflexion separates an actor (often a ReAct agent), an evaluator that produces scalar/textual feedback, and a self-reflection module that writes verbal critiques into an episodic memory buffer that persists across trials, with a configurable num_trials cap as the budget.

The Reflexion reference implementation exposes four explicit memory-strategy options (NONE / LAST_ATTEMPT / REFLEXION / LAST_ATTEMPT_AND_REFLEXION), letting practitioners ablate the contribution of short-term trajectory vs long-term reflection memory.

Tree of Thoughts decomposes problems into 'coherent units of text' (thoughts) and runs deliberate BFS or DFS search over a thought tree, using an LLM evaluator (value or vote scoring) to prune branches and supporting look-ahead and backtracking — making branching factor and depth explicit hyperparameters.

Hugging Face's Open Deep Research argues code-actions reduce step counts by ~30% vs JSON tool-calls (citing Wang et al. 2024) and uses a manager CodeAgent (max_steps=12, planning_interval=4) that delegates to a search_agent ToolCallingAgent (max_steps=20, planning_interval=4) — both step caps and a periodic re-planning interval are explicit.

GPT-Researcher's deep_research skill exposes DEEP_RESEARCH_BREADTH (default 3–4), DEEP_RESEARCH_DEPTH (default 2), and DEEP_RESEARCH_CONCURRENCY (default 4) as configurable knobs, plus a 25,000-word MAX_CONTEXT_WORDS scratchpad cap and trim_context_to_word_limit that keeps the most recent items.

GPT-Researcher's recursion explicitly halves breadth and decrements depth at each level (`new_breadth = max(2, breadth // 2)`, `new_depth = depth - 1`), and constructs the next-level query from the previous research goal plus model-generated follow-up questions — operationalizing the breadth-vs-depth tradeoff as a decaying tree.

GPT-Researcher additionally caps query-expansion iterations (MAX_ITERATIONS=3), sub-topic count (MAX_SUBTOPICS=3), and per-query results (MAX_SEARCH_RESULTS_PER_QUERY=5), and exposes a coarse reasoning_effort knob (low/medium/high) for strategic-LLM cost control.

LangGraph/LangChain Open Deep Research uses a three-phase architecture (scoping → research → final report), where scoping runs a clarification loop with structured output, then writes a research brief that is the only context passed downstream.

In LangGraph Open Deep Research the supervisor is bound to three tool schemas (think_tool, conduct_research, ResearchComplete) but uses a manual tool-execution pattern: conduct_research spawns isolated parallel research subgraphs whose results are returned as compact summaries rather than appended to the supervisor's message history, explicitly to avoid context-window bloat.

LangGraph Open Deep Research stops research via a layered rule: supervisor calls think_tool before every decision and emits ResearchComplete when reflection deems coverage sufficient, but a hard research_iterations counter prevents runaway recursion as a backstop.

An engineering principle stated explicitly in the LangChain Open Deep Research walkthrough is that sub-agents should deliver compressed 'findings/learnings' (information) rather than finished prose, because letting the final report writer compose from raw learnings produces more coherent reports than stitching independently-written paragraphs.

dzhng/deep-research (the same recursive-tree pattern that inspired GPT-Researcher's deep-research mode) takes user-facing query, depth, breadth, and isReport parameters; halves breadth and decrements depth per level; uses an LLM clarification step to ask follow-up questions; and summarizes each branch into 'learnings' before recursing.

OpenDeepResearcher (Shumer) issues 4 parallel search queries per round, performs LLM-based relevance filtering and per-page extraction into a global 'aggregated_contexts' memory, and lets the LLM itself decide whether to issue new queries or emit 'done' — with a maximum-iteration cap as a hard backstop.

DeerFlow uses a hierarchical multi-agent design (coordinator → planner → research_team with researcher and coder sub-agents → reporter), with a maximum plan-count cap and an explicit human-in-the-loop plan-modification step that can route control back to the planner.

A common cross-system recommendation is to keep a multi-round, progressive search that adaptively converges or diverges based on accumulated 'learnings/findings', rather than emitting a single batch of keyword queries — the survey notes this is a converging best practice across closed-source (OpenAI, Gemini, Perplexity, Grok, Qwen) and open-source (DeerFlow, dzhng, langchain, scira, OpenDeepSearch) implementations.

A second cross-system recommendation is to deliver 'cleaner' context between stages — most frameworks deduplicate, rerank, refine, and consolidate retrieval into structured learnings/findings before passing to the report-generation model, rather than dumping raw pages into context.

Human-in-the-loop intent clarification is widely recommended — implementations include OpenAI Deep Research and Qwen Deep Research asking follow-up questions, Gemini Deep Research letting users edit the generated plan, dzhng/deep-research's clarification loop, and DeerFlow's plan-modification step.

disagreements: Iteration-cap defaults vary substantially across implementations and are not standardized: ReAct uses 7 (HotpotQA) / 5 (FEVER) steps; smolagents Open Deep Research uses max_steps=12 (manager) and max_steps=20 (search_agent) with planning_interval=4; GPT-Researcher uses MAX_ITERATIONS=3 (query expansion) and depth=2 (recursion); LangGraph Open Deep Research uses a configurable research_iterations counter without a publicly stated default. Sources do not agree on a single recommended cap.

Architectural choice between single-agent (e.g., OpenAI Deep Research, Grok DeepSearch, Qwen DR per the Exploding-Gradients survey) and multi-agent supervisor+sub-agent (LangGraph Open Deep Research, DeerFlow) is contested: the survey notes multi-agent gives better scalability and parallelism but harder coordination/training, while single-agent benefits from full context memory and end-to-end RL — there is no consensus on which is superior.

Whether to halve breadth at each recursion level is implementation-specific: dzhng/deep-research and GPT-Researcher both halve breadth (`max(2, breadth // 2)`) and decrement depth, whereas Tree-of-Thoughts and LangGraph Open Deep Research keep branching configurable per level without an automatic decay rule. No paper claims one rule is provably better.

Self-RAG's segment-level retrieval threshold δ vs ReAct/Reflexion-style global step caps represent fundamentally different stopping-rule philosophies (learned per-segment soft control vs hard global counter); the literature does not directly compare their cost/quality tradeoffs in a deep-research setting.

findings.sub_question: What are the current best practices for retrieval, browsing, and citation grounding in deep-research agents — including search backend selection, query rewriting, source deduplication and diversity, freshness handling, PDF/JS-rendered page extraction, inline citation styles, and citation-faithfulness metrics such as Attributable to Identified Sources (AIS), citation-F1, and hallucinated-citation detection — based on primary papers and lab engineering posts?
findings.summary:
Across recent surveys, benchmarks, and engineering papers, deep-research agents are converging on a four-stage pipeline (planning → question developing → web exploration → report generation) in which retrieval and citation grounding are no longer single-shot RAG calls but iterative, agent-driven loops [1]. For search backends, frontier systems are split between (a) calling industrial APIs (Bing for OpenAI Deep Research, Google for Gemini Deep Research, a hybrid Bing+Sonar BM25/keyword/dense reranker for Perplexity, X-post access for Grok) and (b) running agentic browsers (WebGPT-style text browsers, Selenium/Playwright-driven DOM agents, and multimodal vision-language agents such as WebVoyager and MM-ReAct that combine screenshots with HTML to handle JS-rendered or visually complex pages) [1]. A surprising recent finding from SAGE is that for current deep-research agents, BM25 still beats reasoning-tuned LLM retrievers (ReasonIR, gte-Qwen2-7B) by ~30% on scientific retrieval, because agents emit short keyword-oriented sub-queries; the proposed fix is corpus-side test-time augmentation (LLM-generated metadata/keywords on documents) rather than fancier retrievers [3]. AgentIR pushes the opposite direction — embedding the agent's natural-language reasoning trace alongside the query yields large gains (BrowseComp-Plus 68% vs. 50% with conventional embeddings, 37% with BM25) [4].

Query rewriting and decomposition is now treated as a learnable 'Question Developing' module. Two paradigms dominate: reward-optimized RL agents (DeepResearcher, Search-R1, R1-Searcher, ZeroSearch, DeepRetrieval, MaskSearch) trained with binary format rewards plus token-F1 or Recall@K/NDCG@K; and richer multi-dimensional rewards that penalize redundant tool calls or reward information gain (InForage, OTC-PO, IKEA, AutoRefine, R-Search) [1]. Supervision-driven alternatives use multi-agent decomposition (ManuSearch, Search-o1, SearchAgent-X) or MCTS+DPO over reasoning trajectories (ReasonRAG) [1]. For browsing, best practice is to interleave parsing, filtering, and re-querying, with a Tavily-style relevance-score threshold (the Static-DRA agent uses 0.30) to drop low-relevance hits before they enter the context [2]. Source deduplication, diversity, and freshness are handled mostly at evaluation time rather than retrieval time: LiveResearchBench's DeepEval explicitly checks for 'duplicate links both inline and in the bibliography' and provider-specific 'grounding redirect' URLs that inflate token counts but not coverage, and it builds tasks that are 'time-varying' (with {{date}} placeholders) so contamination-prone static lookups score lower [5]. The same paper documents recurring failure modes: mismatched in-text citations, missing/broken URLs, inconsistent citation formats, uncited references, broken tables, out-of-order numbering, embedded citations breaking text flow, and outright fabricated data [5].

For citation grounding itself, the dominant inline style — pioneered by WebGPT and codified by Gao et al.'s ALCE — is bracketed numeric citations at sentence end, with statement-level granularity and at most ~3 citations per statement [6][7]. The foundational evaluation framework is Attributable to Identified Sources (AIS) (Rashkin et al. 2023), which formalizes 'according to P, s' attribution using explicatures (context-resolved paraphrases that promote a sentence to a standalone proposition) and a two-stage annotation pipeline: first interpretability (without the source), then attribution (with the source). AIS is binary at the sentence level and validated on QReCC, Wizard-of-Wikipedia, CNN/DM, and ToTTo, with 0.6–0.9 Krippendorff-α inter-annotator agreement [6]. Building on AIS, ALCE introduced automatic Auto-AIS citation precision, recall, and F1 using NLI models like T5-XXL TRUE [7]. AttrScore (Yue et al. 2023, EMNLP findings) refines AIS into a three-way schema — Attributable / Extrapolatory / Contradictory — to distinguish 'no support' from 'direct contradiction', which matters for safety; they show GPT-4 reaches ~85% accuracy on a New-Bing-derived AttrEval-GenSearch test set, but all models still fail systematically on contradictory cases requiring fine-grained numeric or symbolic comparison [7].

The most recent work argues that pure NLI-based citation F1 is insufficient. CiteEval (Xu et al. 2025) shows AIS-style metrics over-credit citations that semantically entail a claim when better sources exist in the retrieval pool, and under-credit partial-but-helpful citations; their fixes are: evaluate against the full retrieval context (not just cited sources), explicitly attribute statements to query/response/parametric contexts so paraphrases of the user query and intra-response reasoning are marked N/A, and rate on a 1–5 Likert scale via 'iterative chain of edits' (delete-misleading, delete-substandard, delete-redundant, add-evidence, add-refinement, add-credibility) — yielding 0.71 Pearson with humans vs. 0.41 for Auto-AIS [8]. LiveResearchBench/DeepEval operationalizes hallucinated-citation detection with an agentic rubric-tree: for each (claim, URL) pair, check (E1) URL resolves, (E2) URL is topically relevant, (E3) content actually supports the claim; on the most search-intensive tasks GPT-5, Grok-4 Deep Research, and Open Deep Research still produce 19–92 citation errors per report, dominated by E3 unsupported-claim hallucinations [5]. DeepEval also separates 'Citation Association' (every claim has some citation, scored as a count-deduction Likert in 0–100) from 'Citation Accuracy' (the citation actually supports the claim), and adopts an LLM-ensemble (Gemini-2.5 Pro + GPT-5) judge after finding Claude-4 Sonnet badly miscalibrated and single-rubric Likert prompts <60% human-aligned [5]. A consistent observation across these works is that multi-agent systems lead on citation-association/discipline, single-agent systems with persistent memory lead on factual/logical consistency, and most current 'deep research' systems are deep searchers (information collectors) rather than deep researchers (insight synthesizers) [5].

key_facts.claim: The canonical deep-research pipeline has four stages — Planning, Question Developing (query formulation), Web Exploration (retrieval/browsing), and Report Generation — and retrieval is iterative and agent-driven rather than single-shot.

Frontier systems split between API-based search backends (Bing for OpenAI Deep Research, Google for Gemini, Bing+Sonar BM25/keyword/dense rerank for Perplexity, X for Grok) and agentic browsers (Selenium/DOM, plus multimodal vision-language agents like WebVoyager and MM-ReAct for JS-rendered or visually complex pages).

BM25 currently outperforms LLM-based reasoning retrievers (ReasonIR, gte-Qwen2-7B) by ~30% in deep-research agent workflows because agents emit keyword-oriented sub-queries; corpus-level test-time augmentation (LLM-generated metadata/keywords on documents) closes much of the gap.

Embedding the agent's natural-language reasoning trace alongside the query (Reasoning-Aware Retrieval, AgentIR-4B) materially improves retrieval accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus (68% vs. 50% with conventional embeddings of double the size, vs. 37% for BM25).

Query-developing strategies divide into reward-optimized RL approaches (DeepResearcher, Search-R1, R1-Searcher, ZeroSearch, DeepRetrieval, MaskSearch) and supervision-driven methods (ManuSearch, Search-o1, SearchAgent-X, ReasonRAG); RL rewards range from format+answer-F1 to multi-dimensional information-gain and tool-cost penalties.

Web-page extraction in practice combines crawlers (Scrapy, BeautifulSoup) for static HTML, headless browsers (Selenium, Playwright) for DOM/JS-rendered pages, and multimodal screenshot+HTML agents (WebVoyager achieves 59% task success using GPT-4V; MM-ReAct embeds screenshots in reasoning chains) for visually complex sites.

Practical deep-research implementations apply a relevance-score threshold to Tavily/Brave search results before passing to the LLM (Static-DRA uses a 0.30 cutoff and keeps the top 5 results) to limit noise and token cost.

The dominant inline citation style is bracketed numeric citations placed at sentence end (e.g., '[1][2][3]'), with most papers (Gao et al. ALCE; CiteEval) adopting a maximum of ~3 citations per statement and treating each citation as a subset of retrieved passages.

Attributable to Identified Sources (AIS) (Rashkin et al. 2023) is the foundational citation-faithfulness framework: a sentence s in context c is AIS iff it is interpretable, its explicature is a standalone proposition, and a generic hearer would affirm 'According to P, s'; it uses a two-stage annotation pipeline (interpretability without the source, then attribution with it).

Citation precision/recall/F1 metrics were operationalized by Auto-AIS / ALCE (Gao et al. 2023): citation recall checks whether the concatenation of cited passages entails the statement via an NLI model (e.g., T5-XXL TRUE); citation precision checks each individual citation for relevance; F1 is their harmonic mean.

AttrScore (Yue et al. 2023) refines AIS into three classes — Attributable, Extrapolatory (insufficient evidence), Contradictory (direct contradiction) — to distinguish hallucination types; on AttrEval-GenSearch (annotated New Bing outputs across 12 domains) GPT-4 reaches ~85% accuracy but all models systematically fail on contradictory cases requiring fine-grained numeric/symbolic comparison.

CiteEval (Xu et al. 2025) argues NLI-based citation evaluation is suboptimal because it ignores uncited but better sources and partial support; its principle-driven framework evaluates citations against the full retrieval context, attributes statements to query/response/parametric contexts (so query paraphrases and intra-response reasoning are marked N/A), and rates citations on a 1–5 Likert with iterative edit actions (delete-misleading/substandard/redundant, add-evidence/refinement/credibility), reaching ~0.71 Pearson with humans vs. ~0.41 for Auto-AIS.

LiveResearchBench's DeepEval performs hallucinated-citation detection via an agentic rubric-tree that for each (claim, URL) pair checks E1 (URL resolves), E2 (URL topically relevant), E3 (content actually supports the claim); top systems (GPT-5, Grok-4 Deep Research, Open Deep Research) still produce 19–92 citation errors per report on search-intensive tasks, dominated by E3 unsupported-claim hallucinations.

DeepEval separates Citation Association (whether every claim has some citation, scored 0–100 with deductions for missing/misplaced citations) from Citation Accuracy (whether the cited URL substantiates the claim), and uses an LLM-ensemble judge (Gemini-2.5 Pro + GPT-5) because single-rubric Likert prompts gave <60% human agreement and Claude-4 Sonnet was inconsistent.

Recurring browsing/citation failure modes documented across systems include mismatched in-text citations and references, missing/incomplete URLs (or provider redirect 'grounding' URLs that inflate token counts), inconsistent citation formats, uncited references in the bibliography, broken table formatting, out-of-order reference numbering, embedded citations that break text flow, and hallucinated/fabricated facts.

Freshness is handled mainly at the task-design level: LiveResearchBench requires tasks to be 'time-varying' (with a {{date}} placeholder resolved at evaluation time) so static, contamination-prone benchmarks score lower; this is one of four explicit benchmark design principles (user-centric, unambiguous, time-varying, multi-faceted/search-intensive).

Empirically, multi-agent deep-research systems lead on Citation Association and Presentation, single-agent web systems lead on Factual & Logical Consistency (because of one persistent memory stream), and almost all systems behave more like deep searchers than deep researchers — only Deerflow+ and Gemini Deep Research outperform Open Deep Research on analysis depth, and even strong systems leave many key statements uncited as response length grows (Pearson 0.679 between length and missing-citation ratio in CiteBench).

Source-quality / 'cite-worthiness' is explicitly out of scope of AIS and Auto-AIS (which only ask whether the cited source supports the statement); CiteEval's 'add-credibility' and 'add-refinement' edit actions are the first attempt to bake source-credibility into citation scoring, complementing trustworthiness with attribution.

disagreements: SAGE [3] reports that BM25 beats LLM-based reasoning retrievers by ~30% on deep-research workflows because agents issue keyword-oriented queries. AgentIR [4] reports the opposite direction — that adding the agent's reasoning trace to the embedding query lifts an open-weight agent from 37% (BM25) to 68%. The two are partly reconcilable (SAGE evaluates off-the-shelf retrievers vs. agent-emitted keywords; AgentIR co-trains the embedding model on synthetic reasoning-augmented queries) but they imply different design recommendations: SAGE favors corpus-side test-time augmentation, AgentIR favors retriever-side reasoning-aware embeddings.

On citation evaluation, AttrScore [7] and Auto-AIS/ALCE [7][8] use NLI-style binary or three-way classification of supportiveness, while CiteEval [8] argues this systematically over- and under-credits citations and pushes a Likert + edit-action framework reaching higher human correlation (0.71 vs ~0.41 Pearson). LiveResearchBench's DeepEval [5] takes a third path — a structured rubric-tree of E1/E2/E3 errors with an LLM ensemble judge — and explicitly notes that holistic 0–10 LLM-as-judge ratings yield <60% human agreement. The community has not converged on a single faithfulness metric.

DeepEval's [5] benchmarking finds that Claude-4 Sonnet exhibits 'inconsistent and low agreement with human experts' as a citation judge, while CiteEval [8] tested GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o and found GPT-4o best — neither paper independently corroborates the other's negative result on Claude, so the relative ranking of judge LLMs is uncertain and likely sensitive to prompt design.

findings.sub_question: Which evaluation benchmarks and protocols are considered authoritative for deep-research agents — specifically BrowseComp, GAIA, FRAMES, Humanity's Last Exam, SimpleQA, FreshQA, and HELM — what does each measure, what scores have leading systems reported, and what LLM-as-judge and human-eval protocols (including regression testing for non-deterministic agents) are documented in their original papers and official leaderboards?

What documented limitations, failure modes, and substantive critiques exist for LLM deep-research systems — including indirect/cross-domain prompt injection (XPIA) from fetched pages, the 'lethal trifecta' exfiltration pattern (Simon Willison), evidence that strong single-agent systems can match or beat multi-agent orchestration, citation hallucination and over-confidence in synthesis, benchmark-gaming on BrowseComp/GAIA, and reported safety incidents or red-team findings in lab system cards from 2024–2026?
findings.summary:
The 2024–2026 literature on LLM deep-research systems converges on a sobering picture: every architectural assumption these systems rely on has documented, often severe failure modes. Prompt injection remains the foundational unsolved problem. Simon Willison's 'lethal trifecta' (June 2025) names the core risk pattern — when an agent simultaneously has (a) access to private data, (b) exposure to untrusted content, and (c) the ability to externally communicate, an attacker who controls any retrieved page can exfiltrate data. Willison documents successful exploits of this pattern against ChatGPT (2023), ChatGPT Plugins, Google Bard, Writer.com, Amazon Q, Google NotebookLM (April 2024), GitHub Copilot Chat (June 2024), Google AI Studio, Microsoft Copilot, Slack, Mistral Le Chat, xAI's Grok, Anthropic's Claude iOS app, ChatGPT Operator (February 2025), and the GitHub MCP server. Meta's 'Agents Rule of Two' (October 2025) generalizes this to state-changing actions; a 14-author paper from OpenAI/Anthropic/Google DeepMind ('The Attacker Moves Second', October 2025) bypassed all 12 published prompt-injection defenses at >90% attack success rate using adaptive attacks, with human red-teamers achieving 100%.

Indirect / cross-domain prompt injection (XPIA) is now empirically widespread on the live web. A 1.2-billion-URL Common Crawl study (Khodayari et al., 2026) found 15,387 validated in-page injection instances across 11,722 pages and 2,042 hosts; 99% use direct task-override, 87% are concealed via CSS/HTML tricks, and 54 templates account for 95% of cases. Effectiveness is 'limited but non-negligible' (0.2%–8% per-attack), but 65% of pages already contained injections 12 months prior, indicating long-lived, structured deployment. Palo Alto Unit 42 (March 2026) catalogued 22 distinct payload techniques in active use, including the first observed AI-ad-review bypass. EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) demonstrated zero-click data exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot via a single crafted email and Markdown-image rendering. Memory-poisoning attacks (Unit 42 against Amazon Bedrock; the MINJA paper at NeurIPS 2025) extend the threat across sessions. QueryIPI (Xie et al., 2025) achieved 70–87% query-agnostic compromise of Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Copilot, and Trae coding agents via tool-description poisoning. OpenAI/Anthropic/Google DeepMind have all publicly stated, by late 2025, that prompt injection cannot be reliably solved within current LLM architectures.

A growing body of controlled work shows strong single-agent systems match or beat multi-agent orchestration on most procedural and reasoning tasks. Tran & Kiela (2025/2026) demonstrate, with an information-theoretic argument grounded in the Data Processing Inequality, that single-agent systems are dominant under fixed thinking-token budgets across Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama, and Gemini 2.5; multi-agent gains in prior literature are largely an artifact of unaccounted compute. Xu et al. (Amazon/UT Austin, 'OneFlow', January 2026) show single-LLM execution of homogeneous workflows matches or exceeds AFlow-designed multi-agent pipelines while reducing cost via KV-cache reuse. Zywot et al. (UvA/ETH/Copenhagen) find that small multi-agent systems can beat much larger single-agent models, but the gain comes almost entirely from orchestrator capacity, not sub-agent capacity, and orchestrator-level reasoning rather than sub-agent reasoning drives improvement. Dennis et al. ('In-Context Prompting Obsoletes Agent Orchestration', 2026) report that a single Claude Sonnet 4.5 with the procedure in its system prompt outperformed a same-model LangGraph orchestrator on all 15 of 15 quality criteria across three procedural domains (p<0.005). Anthropic's own engineering post on multi-agent research systems acknowledges that much of the apparent advantage comes from increased compute. Cemri et al. (2025) catalogue 14 distinct multi-agent failure modes including specification drift, information loss, and misleading evaluation artifacts.

Citation hallucination and over-confident synthesis are pervasive even in retrieval-augmented and 'deep research' modes. Rao, Wong & Callison-Burch (April 2026) measured 3–13% fully hallucinated and 5–18% non-resolving citation URLs across 10 commercial LLMs and deep research agents on DRBench (53,090 URLs) and 168,021 URLs across 32 academic fields on ExpertQA. Critically, deep research agents had the HIGHEST hallucination rates despite generating far more citations per query: Gemini 2.5 Pro Deep Research hallucinated 13.3% of URLs (the worst rate observed). Domain effects vary 2× (5.4% Business → 11.4% Theology), with per-model variation reaching 4.3×. Rao's BibTeX study (April 2026, 931 papers, 3 search-enabled frontier models) found only 50.9% of generated entries are fully correct, with accuracy dropping 27.7 points from popular to recent post-cutoff papers, showing heavy reliance on parametric memory even when search is available. On benchmark gaming and red-team findings, the cross-cutting concern in multiple sources is methodological. The 'Attacker Moves Second' paper's central finding is that static/non-adaptive evaluation of prompt-injection defenses systematically inflates apparent robustness — every defense tested at near-zero ASR was bypassed at >90% under adaptive attack. Cemri et al. emphasize that orchestration can produce misleading benchmark improvements from evaluation artifacts. Multiple sources note that BrowseComp and GAIA, while widely cited, share weaknesses common to agentic benchmarks: ground-truth dependence on a fixed web snapshot, vulnerability to static memorization, and lack of adaptive-attacker conditions. key_facts.claim: Simon Willison coined the 'lethal trifecta' on 16 June 2025: an LLM agent that simultaneously (a) accesses private data, (b) is exposed to untrusted content, and (c) can communicate externally is exploitable for data exfiltration regardless of guardrails.

Documented data-exfiltration prompt-injection exploits against production LLM systems span ChatGPT (April 2023), ChatGPT Plugins, Google Bard, Writer.com, Amazon Q, Google NotebookLM (April 2024), GitHub Copilot Chat (June 2024), Google AI Studio, Microsoft Copilot, Slack, Mistral Le Chat, xAI Grok, Anthropic's Claude iOS app, ChatGPT Operator (February 2025), and the official GitHub MCP server.

EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) is a zero-click prompt-injection exfiltration vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot in which a single crafted email never opened by the user caused Copilot to extract data from OneDrive/SharePoint/Teams via Markdown-image URL exfiltration.

Meta's 'Agents Rule of Two' (October 2025) extends the lethal trifecta by adding state-changing actions, and recommends agents satisfy at most two of: process untrustworthy inputs, access sensitive systems, change state externally.

'The Attacker Moves Second' (October 2025), authored by 14 researchers from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, evaluated 12 published prompt-injection/jailbreak defenses with adaptive attacks and bypassed all of them at >90% attack success rate; human red-teamers achieved 100% across all defenses.

A web-scale empirical study (1.2 billion URLs across 24.8 million hosts, October 2025 Common Crawl) found 15,387 validated indirect prompt-injection instances across 11,722 webpages and 2,042 hosts; 99% use direct task-override, 87% are non-visible, and 54 templates account for 95% of all cases.
Indirect prompt injection is persistent: 65% of pages with injections in October 2025 already contained them 12 months prior; 77% at 6 months; 93% at 3 months.

Per-attack effectiveness of in-the-wild indirect prompt injections is limited but non-negligible: up to 8% on plain-text inputs to small models, dropping to 0.2–1.1% on HTML/raw-response inputs that preserve structural cues.

Palo Alto Unit 42 (March 2026) documented 22 distinct payload-engineering techniques actively used in the wild for indirect prompt injection, with 85.2% relying on social-engineering framing rather than technical override syntax; observed attacker intents include data destruction (rm -rf), DoS (fork bomb), unauthorized transactions, AI ad-review bypass, SEO poisoning, sensitive-information leakage, and system-prompt leakage.

QueryIPI (October 2025) demonstrated query-agnostic indirect prompt injection against five real-world coding agents (Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Copilot, Trae) via malicious MCP tool descriptions, achieving 70–87% success rates in simulation and ~50% transfer to production agents.

Memory-poisoning attacks survive across sessions: Unit 42 demonstrated persistent malicious instructions written into Amazon Bedrock agent memory via crafted webpage URLs, and the MINJA attack (NeurIPS 2025) injected memory records via query-only access to an agent.

Tran & Kiela (2025/2026) prove via the Data Processing Inequality that under fixed thinking-token budgets a single-agent LLM is information-theoretically dominant over multi-agent decompositions, and empirically demonstrate this across Qwen3-30B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, and Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro on FRAMES and MuSiQue 4-hop benchmarks (15 of 15 conditions).

Xu et al. ('OneFlow', Amazon/UT Austin, January 2026) show single-LLM execution of homogeneous multi-agent workflows matches or slightly exceeds AFlow-designed multi-agent counterparts on HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH, HotpotQA, DROP, Shopping-MMLU, and TravelPlanner, with substantial cost reduction from KV-cache reuse.

Zywot et al. (UvA/ETH/Copenhagen, 2026) find on GAIA, GPQA, AIME, MuSiQue, and HLE that small multi-agent systems can beat large single-agent models, but performance is driven primarily by orchestrator capacity rather than sub-agent capacity, and orchestrator-level explicit reasoning yields the largest gains while sub-agent reasoning provides limited or negative benefit.

Dennis et al. (2026) report that a Claude Sonnet 4.5 receiving the full procedure in its system prompt outperforms the same model orchestrated via LangGraph on all 5 quality criteria across all 3 procedural domains (15 of 15 comparisons, p<0.005), with LangGraph failure rates of 9–24% versus 0.5–11.5% for in-context prompting.

Cemri et al. (2025) introduce a 14-mode failure taxonomy for multi-agent LLM systems including specification/planning failures, drift, information loss, and misleading improvements from evaluation artifacts.

Anthropic's own engineering analysis of multi-agent research systems acknowledges that much of the apparent advantage of multi-agent systems over single-agent systems comes from increased compute rather than architectural benefit.
Across 53,090 URLs from 10 commercial LLMs and deep research agents on DRBench, 3–13% of citation URLs are fully hallucinated (no Wayback Machine record) and 5–18% are non-resolving overall.

Deep research agents exhibit higher citation hallucination rates than search-augmented LLMs despite producing far more citations per query: Gemini-2.5-Pro-DeepResearch produced 113.1 URLs per query with a 13.3% hallucination rate (the highest of any system tested), while two pooled deep research agents achieved 10.7% hallucination versus 4.8% for eight search-augmented models.

Across 168,021 URLs and 32 academic fields on ExpertQA, non-resolving rates vary from 5.4% (Business) to 11.4% (Theology); per-model domain variation reaches 4.3× (Claude Sonnet 4.5: 4.0% Mathematics → 17.4% Healthcare/Medicine).

Rao's BibTeX study (April 2026, 931 papers, GPT-5/Claude Sonnet 4.6/Gemini 3 Flash) found 83.6% field-level accuracy but only 50.9% of entries fully correct; accuracy drops 27.7 percentage points from popular (92.7%) to recent post-cutoff (65.0%) papers, demonstrating heavy reliance on parametric memory even when web search is available.

Naser (2026) audited 10 commercially deployed LLMs across 4 domains (69,557 citations) and found a 5× spread in hallucination rates (11.4% GPT-5-mini → 56.8% Anthropic Haiku 4.5); hallucination regressed between Haiku 3.5 (48.8%) and Haiku 4.5 (56.8%), demonstrating that newer models do not necessarily improve citation accuracy.

GhostCite (Xu et al., 2026) benchmarked 13 LLMs across 40 domains (375,000 citations) and reported hallucination rates from 14% to 95%; CiteAudit (Yuan et al., 2026) achieved 97% verification accuracy on synthetic benchmarks but only 90% on real-world cases (GPT-5.2 dropped from 96% to 33% F1).
Sakai et al. (2026) audited 17,842 ACL/NAACL/EMNLP papers from 2024–2025 and identified 295 containing hallucinated references, with a >10× increase from 0.28% of papers in 2024 to 2.59% in 2025.

Ansari (2026) manually coded 100 fabricated citations from 53 NeurIPS 2025 papers and found that 100% exhibited compound failure modes (combining a primary fabrication mechanism with secondary characteristics), explaining why peer review failed to detect them.

Algaba et al. (2024/2025) demonstrated that LLM-generated references show strong popularity bias: among references that exist, ~90% fall in the top 10% most-cited papers in their field, amplifying the Matthew effect via LLM-mediated citation.

Mitigations partially work: urlhealth reduces non-resolving citation URLs by 6–79× to under 1% in agentic self-correction (Rao et al., 2026); CiteGuard achieves 68.1% citation-attribution accuracy approaching human 69.2% (Choi et al., 2026); multi-model consensus filtering raises citation match rates from 16.5% (single model) to 95.6% (k≥3 agreement).

OpenAI's CISO Dane Stuckey (October 2025) publicly acknowledged prompt-injection risks specific to ChatGPT Atlas, and Anthropic's documented adversarial-training results for Claude Opus 4.5 reach approximately 1% prompt-injection attack success rate with Anthropic itself stating '1% still represents meaningful risk' and 'no browser agent is immune to prompt injection'.

The International AI Safety Report 2026 and adaptive-attack literature find that sophisticated attackers bypass best-defended frontier models approximately 50% of the time with just 10 attempts, indicating that 1% per-attempt rates do not translate to robust security at attacker scale.

Standard prompt-injection defenses including Sandwich Defense, Spotlighting variants (Datamarking, Delimiting, Encoding) yield only marginal mitigation against the QueryIPI attack: Sandwich Defense leaves 82% ASR; Spotlighting variants leave 52–84% ASR.

GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023) and BrowseComp are widely used benchmarks for deep-research/agentic systems but the broader red-team literature (notably 'The Attacker Moves Second' and Cemri et al.) finds that static benchmark evaluation systematically overstates robustness, since orchestration and prompting strategies that look strong under fixed test sets fail under adaptive attacks; explicit BrowseComp/GAIA-specific benchmark-gaming critiques exist in concurrent work but were not directly accessible during this investigation.

disagreements: Sources disagree on the magnitude of citation hallucination by model and task: Walters & Wilder (2023) reported 18% (GPT-4) and 55% (GPT-3.5) entirely fabricated; Wu et al. (2025, SourceCheckup) found medical RAG-enabled models avoid URL hallucination, while Rao et al. (2026) report that even RAG/deep-research models hallucinate 3–13% of URLs. The discrepancy reflects domain (medicine vs. broad), elicitation (free-text vs. KR-nat), and verification methodology (post-hoc Wayback vs. content support). Each result is internally consistent within its protocol; cross-study comparison is unreliable absent standardized evaluation.

Sources disagree on whether multi-agent systems are net beneficial: Xu et al., Tran & Kiela, Dennis et al., and Zywot et al. converge that strong single-agent baselines match or beat multi-agent systems under matched compute, while practitioner literature on Anthropic's multi-agent research system reports gains. The reconciliation in the literature is that orchestration helps when (a) effective single-agent context utilization is degraded (Tran & Kiela's degradation experiments), (b) heterogeneous models with complementary strengths are combined, or (c) extra compute is genuinely allocated; otherwise gains are confound by unaccounted compute.

Anthropic and Meta's framings of mitigation differ: Anthropic emphasizes adversarial training reducing per-attempt ASR to ~1%; Meta's Rule of Two and Willison's lethal trifecta argue per-attempt rates are not the right metric and that capability-restriction architectures (CaMeL, FIDES, MELON, Rule of Two) are the only credible direction.
